JSON: Name: psa_headmounted_pipeline Title: Systematic quantification of pupil-size-induced apparent gaze shifts (PSA) and their effects on accuracy, precision, and data loss in head-mounted video-based eye trackers Short Hypothesis: Increasing pupil diameter causes a systematic, measurable apparent gaze shift in head-mounted video-based eye trackers, and the magnitude of that shift scales with the change in pupil diameter. Related Work: Prior work has characterized pupil-size artifacts primarily in desktop video-based eye trackers and documented apparent gaze shifts when pupil diameter changes. Existing gaze-estimation approaches include pupil–corneal-reflection (P-CR) with 2D feature regression, 3D eye models, and appearance-based end-to-end methods; prior evaluations show device- and participant-dependent PSA magnitudes. Limitations in current studies include (1) predominance of desktop-only evaluations, (2) small or non-representative samples, (3) limited exploration of appearance-based head-mounted systems, (4) lack of systematic variation of viewing direction/camera geometry, (5) frequent absence of ground-truth eyeball orientation (e.g., search coil or robotic eye), and (6) closed-source device internals preventing analysis of feature-level shifts (pupil center vs corneal reflection). Existing methods do not provide a standardized pipeline to compare PSA effects across device classes, calibration conditions, and pupil-size ranges nor to quantify secondary impacts on precision and data loss. Abstract: Pupil-size changes produce apparent gaze deviations in video-based eye trackers, yet the prevalence, dose–response relation, and secondary impacts of this pupil-size artifact (PSA) in head-mounted systems remain inadequately quantified. We propose a standardized research pipeline that systematically induces controlled pupil-size changes and measures their effect on reported gaze across multiple head-mounted and desktop eye trackers, including appearance-based and P-CR devices. The pipeline defines experimental luminance manipulations, multi-angle target layouts, calibration variants, data conversions to visual angle, and a set of reproducible quality metrics (apparent gaze shift, accuracy, STD and RMS sample-to-sample precision, and data loss). The contribution is a device-agnostic protocol, a minimal ground-truth validation procedure using an artificial eye or coil, and a prespecified statistical analysis framework to estimate dose–response curves and device-specific PSA signatures. Expected outcomes include quantification of PSA magnitudes, characterization of how PSA degrades spatial accuracy and precision, and a comparison of appearance-based versus feature-based systems under matched conditions. Experiments: Participants and datasets: recruit N=30 adult participants with normal or corrected binocular vision; additionally use an artificial eye rig and, where feasible, a scleral search coil ground-truth dataset (single-subject coil or robotic eye). Eye trackers: Pupil Core, Pupil Neon (appearance-based), SMI ETG 2w, Tobii Pro Glasses 2, and SR Research EyeLink 1000 Plus (desktop reference). Stimuli and pupil manipulation: central fixation target plus a 3x3 grid of peripheral fixation targets spanning ±10° horizontally/vertically; three luminance conditions: bright (white display), dark (black display), and continuous sinusoidal luminance sweep (0→100% and back over 30 s) to sample pupil diameter range; additionally present 5-ms flash pulses for transient large pupil responses. Calibration variants: perform calibration under bright and dark conditions for each device (two calibration modes). Data collection: three repeats per target × luminance condition × calibration mode; record binocular gaze, pupil area/diameter, corneal reflection coordinates, and scene camera images when available; sampling rates as device permits (≥50 Hz). Baselines: device native gaze outputs; ground truth from artificial eye or coil. Evaluation metrics: apparent gaze shift (mean Euclidean difference in degrees between matched bright/dark conditions and along luminance sweep), spatial accuracy (mean absolute offset degrees to target), precision STD (deg) and RMS-S2S (deg), data loss (% invalid samples), and correlation between pupil diameter change and reported gaze displacement. Statistical analyses: linear mixed-effects models with fixed effects pupil_diameter_change, device, calibration_mode, gaze_direction, and random intercepts for participant; paired tests for within-subject bright vs dark; compute effect sizes and 95% CIs; Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc contrasts. Ablation/comparison studies: (A) appearance-based (Pupil Neon) vs P-CR devices controlling for sampling rate and calibration mode; (B) calibration bright vs dark; (C) inclusion vs removal of corneal reflection input (where raw signals available); (D) viewing-direction sweep to map PSA as function of camera-eye angle. Ground-truth validation: compare device-reported shifts against artificial eye/coil to confirm artifact (non-ocular rotation) vs real eye movement. Data processing pipeline: standardized frame-undistortion, marker-based scene-to-screen mapping, trimming first/last 12.5% of trials, outlier removal (>3 SD or >10°), convert to visual degrees using measured geometry. Success criteria: significant positive correlation between pupil diameter increase and apparent gaze shift across devices and reproducible device-specific dose–response curves; device ranking by PSA magnitude and quantification of secondary effects on accuracy and precision. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: inability to access raw pupil or corneal-reflection coordinates for closed-source devices limits mechanism analysis; sensor saturation or automatic camera exposure/gain changes during luminance sweeps may confound pupil measurements; artificial eye/coil setups may not replicate biological pupil-center shifts or eyelid interactions. Data and evaluation biases: participant heterogeneity in pupil reactivity and fixation stability introduces inter-subject variance; calibrations performed under only two conditions may not generalize to intermediate ambient lighting. Scalability and compute: high-volume scene-camera image processing and undistortion for multiple devices increases storage and compute requirements; real-time synchronization across heterogeneous devices may be challenging. Limits to generalization: results obtained with the selected devices and display geometries may not transfer to other head-mounted systems, AR/VR displays, or mobile real-world environments; short-term laboratory-induced pupil changes may differ from dynamic, cognitive- or task-driven pupil variations in naturalistic tasks. Statistical limitations: mixed-effects estimates may be sensitive to sample size and unbalanced device availability (e.g., fewer Tobii sessions).
